newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: MARKET PLEASANTLY SURPRISED BY NEW DUTCH 2007 BOND.
newsitem.headline: MARKET PLEASANTLY SURPRISED BY NEW DUTCH 2007 BOND.

text.p: The Dutch bond market was pleasantly surprised on Friday by a new government bond issue which met its needs rather than its expectations.

The state had been widely tipped to reopen sales of its 5.75 percent September 2002 issue, topping up the outstanding 7.5 billion guilders to take it over the 10 billion mark which is generally seen as the critical mass needed for benchmark status.
But the Finance Ministry said it would hold tap sales next week of a new 5.75 percent bond due February 2007 -- the first new 10-year Dutch state loan for more than a year.

"We had thought a re-opening of the five-year benchmark, the September 2002 bond, was very likely, but on the other hand the market was looking for a new 10-year benchmark," said Niels Kortleve, fixed income analyst at Rabobank.
The government's previous 10-year bond, the 6.00 percent January 2006 issue, now had a remaining life of nine years, making it less suitable for benchmarking purposes, he said.
Kortleve said the Dutch market might have fallen out of favour in the absence of a fresh, liquid 10-year benchmark.
"Quite a lot of international investors only look at the long end of the curve, at the 10-year benchmarks," he said.

Kortleve said, depending on how strong demand for the new bond proved when sales open next week, the government might decide to go for a haul of 10 billion guilders or more in one fell swoop or sell a second tranche later in the year.
A re-opening of the September 2002 bond later this year also remained likely, he added.
Dutch government bond issues have become something of a rarity, with the state tapping the market only six times in the whole of 1996 and just once in the second half of that year.
The government continues to publish an official estimate of its 1997 borrowing requirement of 33.5 billion guilders, but government bond issuance this year is expected to be far lower.

The Finance Ministry said on Friday that the state's call on the capital market this year would be reduced by 14.35 billion guilders as a result of a corresponding reduction in a cash balance previously held with the central bank.

This and other factors are likely to lead to just a handful of Dutch state loans this year. Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm is expected to shed more light on government finances and borrowing in a progress report on the 1997 budget due by early May.
